title: Denominator
summary: The denominator is the bottom number of a fraction. It tells how many equal parts the whole is split into — in 3/4, the denominator 4 means the whole is divided into 4 equal parts. The bigger the denominator, the smaller each part.

processes: Splitting a whole into equal parts
plainLanguageExplanation: The denominator is the bottom number of a fraction. It tells you how many equal parts the whole is divided into. In 3/4, the denominator 4 means the pizza is cut into 4 equal slices; the numerator 3 says you take three of them. A bigger denominator means MORE cuts, so each part is SMALLER — a sixth (1/6) is smaller than a half (1/2). So when two fractions have the same numerator, the one with the larger denominator is smaller: 1/3 < 1/2. The denominator literally 'denominates' or names the parts — it says what kind of pieces you are counting.

whyItMatters: The denominator decides the size of every piece in a fraction. Understanding it correctly prevents the classic mistake of thinking 1/5 is bigger than 1/3, and it is essential for comparing, adding, and simplifying fractions.
tagline: The bottom number that sizes the parts
didYouKnow: The word 'denominator' comes from the Latin 'denominare', meaning 'to name' — the denominator names the parts, telling you they are fourths, sixths, or tenths.
compareReason: Numerator and denominator answer opposite questions — one counts parts, the other sizes them — so comparing the pair makes each clear.
